claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase microstructure consisting of a ductile FCC matrix and a hard B2 intermetallic phase.
The alloy forms an initially protective oxide layer under static conditions.
Mechanical abrasion under simultaneous wear and corrosion preferentially removes the protective oxide film at FCC/B2 phase boundaries.
Oxide removal exposes compositional and electrochemical heterogeneities between the FCC and B2 phases.
The exposed heterogeneities form localized micro-galvanic cells.
Localized micro-galvanic cells accelerate corrosion at FCC/B2 interfaces.
Corrosion-induced weakening of FCC/B2 interfaces further accelerates wear.
The mutual acceleration of corrosion and wear creates a self-reinforcing degradation cycle.
The combined degradation exceeds the simple sum of independently acting wear and corrosion.
FCC/B2 boundaries contain concentrated stress fields in addition to compositional and electrochemical differences.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce approximately 50% higher total degradation than wear-only or corrosion-only baselines.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will increase the wear rate by roughly 30% because oxide-film loss exposes softer regions.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will increase pitting or interfacial corrosion damage by up to 40%.
Pre-passivation or pre-oxidation that stabilizes the oxide film will mitigate overall degradation.

The proposed mechanism applies to dual-phase FCC/B2 eutectic high-entropy alloys near 350°C in chloride-containing environments when mechanical loading repeatedly disrupts the oxide without causing catastrophic failure.
Other high-temperature oxidation processes may also contribute to degradation.
